title: Rubin Observatory Unveils First Dwarf Planet Candidate in Our Solar System, Phys.org Reports
body:
Scientists working with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have identified a distant, icy world that could soon join the exclusive club of dwarf planets in the Solar System. The object, provisionally designated 2026 ED138, was detected in data from the observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and appears to orbit the Sun well beyond Pluto, placing it among the most remote members of our planetary family. If follow‑up observations confirm its size and dynamical properties, the new body would become the latest addition to a roster that currently includes Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake, and a handful of other trans‑Neptunian objects.

The discovery emerged from a meticulous search of LSST data conducted by Dr. Aisha Karim, an astronomer at the University of Arizona, who was sifting through images collected during the survey’s first month of operation. The object was first flagged as a faint moving source in a series of exposures taken in early March, and subsequent analysis revealed a slow, retrograde motion consistent with an orbit far beyond the Kuiper Belt. Preliminary orbital calculations suggest a semi‑major axis of roughly 120 astronomical units, a period of more than 1,300 Earth years, and an inclination that nudges it out of the ecliptic plane. Its brightness, combined with an estimated albedo typical of icy bodies, points to a diameter in the range of 600 to 800 kilometres—large enough to satisfy the International Astronomical Union’s (IAU) criterion that a dwarf planet must be massive enough for its self‑gravity to pull it into a near‑spherical shape.

The potential inclusion of 2026 ED138 raises intriguing questions about the architecture of the outer Solar System. Objects of this size and distance have historically been hard to detect, hidden in the glare of the Sun and the vastness of space. The Rubin Observatory’s LSST, with its unprecedented wide‑field imaging capability and rapid cadence, is designed to change that. By repeatedly scanning the entire southern sky every few nights, LSST can spot faint, slow‑moving objects that eluded earlier surveys such as the Dark Energy Survey and the Pan‑STARRS program. Dr. Karim notes that “the sheer volume of high‑quality data we now have opens a new frontier for discovering the hidden population of distant worlds, and 2026 ED138 is likely just the tip of the iceberg.”

If the object’s dimensions are confirmed, it would also have implications for theories of planetary formation and migration. Some models predict a substantial reservoir of planetesimals beyond the Kuiper Belt—often referred to as the “inner Oort cloud”—that never coalesced into larger planets. The presence of a dwarf‑planet‑sized body in this region would support the idea that the early Solar System possessed enough material at great distances to form sizable icy worlds, only to leave them stranded in distant, eccentric orbits after the giant planets migrated outward. Moreover, the object's orbital tilt could hint at past gravitational interactions, perhaps with the hypothesized Planet Nine or with passing stars during the Sun’s birth cluster phase.

The next steps involve securing precise measurements of the object's size, shape, and composition. Astronomers plan to use the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope to obtain high‑resolution imaging and spectroscopy, which will reveal surface ices, possible atmospheres, and rotational characteristics. Ground‑based facilities equipped with adaptive optics, such as the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope, will also contribute to refining its orbit and mass estimates. Only after a comprehensive suite of observations can the International Astronomical Union formally recognize 2026 ED138 as a dwarf planet.

The identification of 2026 ED138 underscores the transformative power of the Rubin Observatory’s LSST and heralds a new era of discovery at the Solar System’s frontier. As the survey continues to collect data over the coming decade, astronomers anticipate uncovering many more hidden worlds, each offering fresh clues about the Solar System’s distant past and its dynamic evolution. Whether 2026 ED138 will secure a permanent place among the dwarf planets remains to be seen, but its emergence already expands our view of the Sun’s far‑flung companions and sets the stage for future breakthroughs in planetary science.
